title: Λέων καὶ Προμηθεὺς καὶ ἐλέφας
titleEn: The Lion, Prometheus and the Elephant
part: The Lion, Prometheus and the Elephant (Chambry 210)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 210. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων κατεμέμφετο Προμηθέα πολλάκις ὅτι μέγαν αὐτὸν ἔπλασε καὶ καλόν, καὶ τὴν μὲν γένυν ὥπλισε τοῖς ὀδοῦσι, τοὺς δὲ πόδας ἐκράτυνε τοῖς ὄνυξιν, ἐποίησέ τε τῶν ἄλλων θηρίων δυνατώτερον· « ὁ δὲ τοιοῦτος, ἔφασκε, τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα φοβοῦμαι. »
sentences.tr: Leōn katemempheto Promēthea pollakis hoti megan auton eplase kai kalon, kai tēn men genyn hōplise tois odousi, tous de podas ekratyne tois onyxin, epoiēse te tōn allōn thēriōn dynatōteron· « ho de toioutos, ephaske, ton alektryona phoboumai. »
sentences.l: A lion often found fault with Prometheus, because he had moulded him great and beautiful, and had armed his jaw with teeth and strengthened his feet with claws, and had made him mightier than the other beasts ; « and being such as I am, » he kept saying, « I am afraid of the cock. »
sentences.i: A lion was forever finding fault with Prometheus: he had moulded him great and beautiful, had armed his jaw with teeth and strengthened his feet with claws, and had made him mightier than the other beasts — « and for all that, » he kept saying, « I am afraid of the cock. »
sentences.n: Prometheus is the moulder of living creatures in this collection, and πλάσσω is the potter's word, to shape out of clay. The ὅτι clause states the grounds of the complaint, which are all in the lion's favour — the grievance only arrives in the quotation. τῶν ἄλλων θηρίων is a genitive of comparison after the comparative. Chambry prints the quotation opening in the middle of the sentence with a lower-case ὁ δέ.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ Προμηθεὺς ἔφη· « Τί με μάτην αἰτιᾷ ; τὰ γὰρ ἐμὰ πάντα ἔχεις ὅσα πλάττειν ἐδυνάμην· ἡ δέ σου ψυχὴ πρὸς τοῦτο μόνον μαλακίζεται. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho Promētheus ephē· « Ti me matēn aitiāi ; ta gar ema panta echeis hosa plattein edynamēn· hē de sou psychē pros touto monon malakizetai. »
sentences.l: And Prometheus said: « Why do you blame me in vain? For you have all that is mine, as much as I was able to mould ; but your spirit goes soft in the face of this one thing alone. »
sentences.n: The craftsman's defence is a division of labour: the body was his to make, the ψυχή is not. μαλακίζομαι is to be made soft, and is the ordinary word for courage giving way.

sentences.t: Ἔκλαιεν οὖν ἑαυτὸν ὁ λέων καὶ τῆς δειλίας κατεμέμφετο καὶ τέλος ἀποθανεῖν ἤθελεν.
sentences.tr: Eklaien oun heauton ho leōn kai tēs deilias katemempheto kai telos apothanein ēthelen.
sentences.l: So the lion wept for himself and found fault with his own cowardice, and at last wanted to die.
sentences.n: κατεμέμφετο returns from the first sentence, but with a genitive now, τῆς δειλίας, the thing blamed, where before it had the accusative of the person blamed. τέλος stands adverbially, 'in the end'.

sentences.t: Οὕτω δὲ γνώμης ἔχων ἐλέφαντι περιτυγχάνει, καὶ προσαγορεύσας εἱστήκει διαλεγόμενος, καὶ ὁρῶν διαπαντὸς τὰ ὦτα κινοῦντα· « Τί πάσχεις ; ἔφη, καὶ τί ποτε οὐδὲ μικρὸν ἀτρεμεῖ σου τὸ οὖς ; »
sentences.tr: Houtō de gnōmēs echōn elephanti peritynchanei, kai prosagoreusas heistēkei dialegomenos, kai horōn diapantos ta ōta kinounta· « Ti pascheis ; ephē, kai ti pote oude mikron atremei sou to ous ; »
sentences.l: And being thus minded, he comes upon an elephant, and having greeted him stood talking with him, and seeing him moving his ears the whole time: « What is the matter with you? » he said, « and why ever does your ear not keep still even a little? »
sentences.i: In this frame of mind he comes upon an elephant, greets him and stands talking, and seeing him move his ears the whole time says: « What ails you? And why on earth will your ear not keep still even for a moment? »
sentences.n: οὕτω γνώμης ἔχων is the idiom of ἔχω with an adverb and a genitive of respect: 'to be so situated as regards judgement', that is, in this state of mind. The present περιτυγχάνει sits beside the pluperfect εἱστήκει of ἵστημι, which in that tense means simply 'he stood'. κινοῦντα is accusative, agreeing with the elephant as the object of ὁρῶν.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ ἐλέφας, κατὰ τυχὴν περιπτάντος αὐτῷ κώνωπος· « Ὁρᾷς, ἔφη, τοῦτο τὸ βραχύ, τὸ βομβοῦν ; ἢν εἰσδύνῃ μου ⟨τῇ⟩ τῆς ἀκοῆς ὁδῷ, τέθνηκα. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho elephas, kata tychēn periptantos autōi kōnōpos· « Horāis, ephē, touto to brachy, to bomboun ; ēn eisdynēi mou ⟨tēi⟩ tēs akoēs hodōi, tethnēka. »
sentences.l: And the elephant, a gnat having by chance flown round about him: « Do you see, » he said, « this small thing, the buzzing one? If it slips in by ⟨the⟩ road of my hearing, I am dead. »
sentences.i: And the elephant — a gnat had just then flown round him — said: « Do you see this little thing, the one that buzzes? If it works its way in by ⟨the⟩ passage of my ear, I am done for. »
sentences.n: ⟨τῇ⟩ in angle brackets is Chambry's own supplement, a word he adds to complete the construction; the square brackets elsewhere in this collection mean the opposite, words he deletes. ἤν is ἐάν contracted, and with the subjunctive gives the vivid future condition; the apodosis is the perfect τέθνηκα, 'I am already a dead thing', not a future. Chambry prints κατὰ τυχήν with the accent on the last syllable, where the usual accentuation is τύχην; the reading is left as the page has it.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ λέων· « Τί οὖν ἔτι ἀποθνῄσκειν, ἔφη, με δεῖ τοσοῦτον ὄντα καὶ ἐλέφαντος εὐτυχέστερον ὅσῳ κρείττων κώνωπος ὁ ἀλεκτρυών ; »
sentences.tr: Kai ho leōn· « Ti oun eti apothnēiskein, ephē, me dei tosouton onta kai elephantos eutychesteron hosōi kreittōn kōnōpos ho alektryōn ; »
sentences.l: And the lion: « Why then must I still die, » he said, « being so great, and more fortunate than an elephant by as much as the cock is stronger than a gnat? »
sentences.i: And the lion said: « Why then should I die after all, being as great as I am, and better off than an elephant by just as much as a cock is mightier than a gnat? »
sentences.n: ὅσῳ is a dative of the degree of difference with the comparative εὐτυχέστερον; its answering τοσούτῳ is left unexpressed. τοσοῦτον is accusative, agreeing with με through ὄντα. ἐλέφαντος and κώνωπος are both genitives of comparison. The reasoning is exact and completely upside down.

sentences.t: Ὁρᾷς ὅσον ἰσχύος ὁ κώνωψ ἔχει, ὡς καὶ ἐλέφαντα φοβεῖν.
sentences.tr: Horāis hoson ischyos ho kōnōps echei, hōs kai elephanta phobein.
sentences.l: You see how much of strength the gnat has, so as to frighten even an elephant.
sentences.n: This closing turns to the reader in the second person rather than using one of the collection's usual 'the story shows' formulas. ὅσον ἰσχύος is a partitive genitive, 'how much of strength'; ὡς with the infinitive states the result.
